opus-5.5.text:
That's a really interesting direction, and honestly I think there's a lot of potential there. Right now, when we work with model zoos and try to learn from weights directly, we're mostly treating the weights as raw vectors, flattening them and feeding them into some encoder. That works surprisingly well, but it ignores a lot of the structure that's inherent in neural networks.

Take permutation symmetry as an example. You can shuffle the neurons in a hidden layer, permute the incoming and outgoing weights accordingly, and you have exactly the same function, yet in weight space it looks like a completely different point. So if you learn directly on raw weights, your model has to figure out these equivalences on its own, which is data-hungry and inefficient.

Transforming the weights into another domain first is one way to deal with that. You could think of something like a frequency-domain representation, similar to what we do with signals and images, where certain properties become much more apparent. Or you could map the network into a graph representation, where neurons are nodes and weights are edges, so you get permutation equivariance more or less for free. Some people have also looked at canonicalization, bringing all networks into an aligned form before learning.

What makes this exciting is that the right representation could make the downstream tasks much easier: predicting a model's accuracy or generalization gap, detecting whether it was trained on a certain dataset or backdoored, or even generating new weights for initialization. In our hyper-representation work we saw that the learned latent space already captures a lot of these properties, but I'm convinced a smarter input transformation would make it more robust and scale better to larger architectures.

So I see it as a very promising step. Weights are a data modality in their own right, and just like in vision or audio, finding the right representation before learning is probably half the battle.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, that's actually a really interesting question, and it's something we've been thinking about quite a bit in the context of our work on what we call "weight space learning" or treating populations of neural networks as a data modality in their own right.

So let me step back for a second. The basic idea we started with is: if you train, say, thousands of small neural networks on some task, each of them ends up with a weight vector. And the question is, can you learn something about those networks—their accuracy, their generalization gap, what data they were trained on, whether they've been backdoored—just by looking at the weights? And it turns out you can, which was already kind of surprising to us.

But the raw weight space is a nasty place to learn in. You have these huge dimensionalities, you have all the permutation symmetries—you can swap two neurons in a hidden layer and get a functionally identical network with a completely different weight vector—and you have scaling symmetries with ReLU activations and so on. So learning directly on the flattened weights means your model has to somehow discover all these invariances on its own, which is wasteful and often just doesn't work well.

So that's where the transformation idea comes in. If we can map the weights into some other representation where those symmetries are already accounted for, or where the structure is more amenable to our learning algorithms, we should get a much better starting point. And there are a few directions people are exploring there.

One is to go to a sort of canonical or aligned form—you align networks to a reference so the permutation ambiguity is removed before you ever look at them. Another is to use architectures that are equivariant to those symmetries by construction, so graph neural networks or set-based approaches where the neurons are treated as nodes and the weights as edges. And then a third direction, which I personally find really exciting, is to think about the weights in terms of what the network does rather than what it is—so you probe the network with inputs and look at the outputs, or you look at the function it implements, and that becomes your representation. In a sense that's a transformation into function space.

And then there's the more learned approach, which is what we did with hyper-representations—you train an autoencoder on the population of weights and learn a latent space, and that latent space turns out to be very useful. You can predict properties from it, you can sample new weights from it, and the embedding of a network ends up being more semantically meaningful than the weights themselves.

So I think the potential is huge, honestly. What we're really after is a representation where the geometry corresponds to something meaningful—where networks that are close in the embedding space actually behave similarly. If you have that, then a lot of things open up: model zoos become searchable, you can do transfer learning at the level of entire models, you can generate initializations that are already in a good region of the loss landscape. It's early days, but I think transforming weights into a better domain before learning is going to be one of the key ingredients for making all of that practical.

astra-6.text:
I think that’s a very interesting direction, because the weight space itself is quite difficult to work with. Two neural networks can implement the same function but have different weights—for example, because you permute the neurons in a hidden layer. So if you simply compare those weights directly, you might conclude that the networks are very different, even though their behavior is identical.

By transforming the weights into another representation, you have an opportunity to capture properties that are more meaningful than individual parameter values. Can we learn a representation that tells us something about the network’s performance, its generalization, or the task it was trained on? And can we then use that representation to transfer knowledge between networks?

The important question is what information that transformation preserves. You want to remove irrelevant variation without losing the structure that determines what the network actually does. If we can get that right, then we can start treating trained networks themselves as data—and learn across a population of models.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that’s a very interesting direction, because the weights are a representation of what a neural network has learned, but they’re not necessarily in a form that is easy for another model to work with. For example, you can permute neurons and change the weight representation without changing the function of the network. So a distance between two sets of weights doesn’t automatically tell you how similar their behavior is.

If we can transform those weights into a representation that captures the meaningful structure, then we can start learning about entire networks. We could ask whether a model will generalize well, what kinds of tasks it might be useful for, or which models are good starting points for transfer learning.

The important question is what information that transformation preserves. We want to remove irrelevant differences while retaining the information that explains the model’s behavior. If we can do that, we have a way of using the knowledge already contained in trained networks to guide the training of new ones.

r001.rationale: The response discusses transforming network weights to preserve meaningful structure, but does not propose adding high-frequency information to refine blurry generated weights.
